To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the performance of scene classification is highly sensitive to the representation of the image, that the performance of the best scene classification algorithm (linear SVM) can be significantly improved by choosing the best representation, and that the best representations are based on a small subset of the original visual words.

(1) a visual-word representation can be designed that is as good as, and sometimes better than, state-of-the-art representations for scene classification; (2) this representation is obtained by combining a few simple and intuitive techniques; (3) this representation has the potential to be used in many other computer vision applications.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to represent a visual image in terms of visual words in order to perform scene classification.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

1) the choice of the visual-word representation is very important, 2) the performance can be improved by using the visual-word representation that is more similar to the bag-of-word representation of text documents and 3) the performance can also be improved by using a visual-word representation that has a higher dimension.

the best performance is achieved when a large number of visual words are extracted from a large vocabulary, and when the visual words are weighted by the number of occurrences of each word in the image.

, the best performance is achieved by using a combination of different weighting schemes, and that, the best weighting schemes are those that use the local image statistics to weight the importance of the visual words.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the best performance is achieved by using a relatively small number of visual words, and that the best performance can be achieved by using the same visual-word selection for all images in the collection, which is the case for our "best" representation, the TFIDF-LSH representation.

1) a small subset of visual words can be selected to represent an image with little loss of information; 2) the weighting of visual words is crucial to the performance of the bag-of-visual-word representation; and 3) the performance can be further improved by using a combination of different weighting methods.
a simple bag of visual words with term weighting and dimension reduction can produce a good representation for scene classification.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a good visual-word representation for a particular classification task can be obtained by applying a few simple techniques to a set of candidate representations.

the choice of visual word representation has a significant impact on the scene classification performance, and that the performance of a visual-word based representation is highly dependent on the choice of the dimension and weighting of the visual words.
